raw_findings.message: An item with an empty `locations` slice causes a divide-by-zero panic when its reorder point is computed.
A GET request to `/items` leaves `pathParts` too short and panics when this handler indexes element 3.
`io.ReadAll` reads the entire item request body without a size limit, so a local client can exhaust server memory with a sufficiently large POST.
The JSON unmarshal error is ignored, so malformed input such as `{` creates and stores an item with zero-value fields and returns success.
Creating an item without a supplier leaves `item.Supplier` nil, and fetching or reporting that item panics when this line reads its name.
A negative reservation quantity passes the stock check and increases stock while reducing reserved inventory.
Releasing more than the reserved quantity makes reserved inventory negative and adds the unreserved excess to stock.
The `int32` multiplication can overflow for large pack values and make a restock unexpectedly reduce or corrupt stock.
An out-of-range or negative `limit` causes a slice-bounds panic, so a request such as `/report?limit=100` can fail this handler.
The handler computes matching items but returns only the query string, so searches never return the matching inventory records.
The unescaped `q` parameter is inserted into an HTML response, allowing a crafted search URL to execute attacker-supplied markup or script.
The reset endpoint's authentication token is a fixed source-code constant, allowing anyone who can inspect the code to authenticate and clear the inventory.
Each request opens `requests.log` without closing the file, so repeated requests can exhaust the server's file descriptors.
`Get` returns a shared item pointer after releasing the lock, allowing concurrent handlers to race on fields and lose updates or accept reservations against stale stock.

fixed_raw_findings.message: SKU values are accepted without newline validation and written directly to the movement log, so a SKU containing a newline can forge additional log entries.
The decoder accepts the first JSON value without checking for EOF, so a request containing a valid item followed by extra JSON or garbage is accepted as a successful creation.
The item pointer is stored before it is encoded in the response, so a concurrent update to the same SKU can mutate it while the JSON encoder reads it, causing a data race or inconsistent response.
Adding the released quantity to stock can overflow int32; for example, restock stock to MaxInt32 while a reservation remains, then release that reservation.
The handler computes and sorts matching items but returns only the escaped query, so search requests never return the matching inventory records.
The decoded request path is written to the audit log without neutralizing line breaks, so a path containing an encoded newline can forge additional log entries.

raw_findings.message: Rendering an item with an empty `locations` slice divides by zero and panics.
A GET request to `/items` produces too few path components for index 3 and panics instead of returning a client error.
The handler reads the entire request body without a size limit, allowing a client to consume excessive memory with a large body.
The JSON unmarshal error is ignored, so malformed item JSON is accepted and can create an unintended zero-valued item.
Rendering an item whose supplier is nil dereferences `item.Supplier` and panics.
A negative reserve quantity passes the stock check and increases stock while decreasing the reserved quantity.
The release quantity is not checked against the reserved amount, so releasing too much makes `reserved` negative and inflates stock.
The `int32` multiplication and stock addition can overflow for large restock values, producing an incorrect wrapped stock count.
Negative pack counts or pack sizes are accepted and can make a restock reduce stock.
A negative or greater-than-item-count `limit` slices outside the available items and panics.
The search query is inserted into an HTML response without escaping, so a query containing markup or script executes in a browser.
The handler computes matching items but responds only with the query, so callers never receive the search results.
The reset endpoint's authorization token is a constant in source, so anyone with access to the source can send it and clear the inventory.
Each successfully opened request log file is left open, so repeated requests can exhaust the server's file descriptors.
Creating an item with an existing SKU silently replaces it, which can erase its current stock and reservations.
`Get` returns a mutable item pointer after releasing the store lock, allowing concurrent handlers to race on item fields and lose or corrupt inventory updates.

A SKU containing `/` is accepted here, but the item GET handler rejects paths containing `/`, leaving the created item unreachable through its documented lookup endpoint.
Creating an item with an existing SKU silently replaces its record, so a repeated request can discard the existing stock and reserved quantities.
This addition has no overflow check; after reserving stock and restocking while a reservation remains, releasing it can wrap stock to a negative value.
The handler computes matching items but returns only the escaped query, so searches never return the inventory results the endpoint promises.
The decoded request path is written to the audit log without escaping, so a path containing an encoded newline can forge additional log entries.

raw_findings.message: The user-controlled SKU is written verbatim to the movement log, so an SKU containing newlines can forge additional log entries.
A request such as `GET /items` produces too few path parts and panics at this index, causing the request to fail instead of returning a client error.
The handler reads the entire request body without a size limit, so a client can exhaust server memory by sending an oversized item request.
JSON decoding errors are ignored, so malformed or non-JSON bodies are accepted as zero-valued item data and stored.
An item with an empty locations slice causes `reorderPoint` to divide by zero when this view is generated, such as on `GET /items/{sku}` or a report.
Creating an item without a supplier leaves this pointer nil, and viewing that item dereferences it and panics.
Movement quantities and restock counts are not validated as nonnegative, so negative values can increase stock or reduce reservations in unintended ways.
Concurrent requests can read and modify the same item fields without synchronization, causing data races and lost updates or overselling during reservations.
A release larger than the reserved quantity is accepted, allowing `Reserved` to become negative while stock is increased.
The `int32` pack multiplication and stock addition can overflow, so large restock values can wrap around and produce an incorrect or negative stock count.
The parsed limit is not checked against the item count or for negative values, so an out-of-range or negative limit panics when slicing.
The search query is inserted into an HTML response without escaping, so a request containing markup such as a script tag returns executable content.
The handler computes matching items but responds with only the raw query, so searches never return the matching inventory records.
The reset credential is embedded in source code, allowing anyone who can inspect the code to obtain the token and clear the inventory.
A new request-log file descriptor is opened for every request and never closed, so repeated requests can exhaust the process's file descriptors.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The JSON decoder has no request-size limit, so a client can submit a huge item body that requires excessive memory and can exhaust the service.
The reservation, release, and restock handlers do not check the HTTP method, so a request using GET or another method with a JSON body can still mutate inventory.
Releasing adds to Stock without checking int32 overflow; after reserving stock and restocking while a reservation remains, a valid release can wrap Stock negative.
The handler computes matching items but returns only the escaped query, so every search request omits the results it is documented to provide.
The reset handler accepts any HTTP method, so an authorized GET request can perform the destructive reset despite the endpoint being documented as POST.
The raw URL path is written to the audit log without neutralizing newlines, so a request path containing an encoded newline can forge additional log entries.
